Studies on Switchable Stability of Pickering Emulsions

Abstract:

Dispersions of fine drops of one liquid in continuous phase of another immiscible liquid results in emulsion systems with high liquid-liquid interfacial area, useful in interphase mass transfer and heterogeneous reaction engineering. Surfactants with quantified HLB (hydrophilic lipophilic balance) have been traditionally used to stabilize such emulsion systems. However, the toxicity and short-term stability due to energetic considerations challenges the use of classical emulsions for drug delivery and other bio-medical applications. On the other hand, the Pickering emulsions in which surfactants are replaced by solid nanoparticles have potential to offer not only superior stability and tuneability but also switchable stability. In this work, we report our studies on stability aspects of silica and starch nanoparticle stabilized Pickering emulsion system with dispersed phase formed by non-polar liquid solubilizing the lipophilic drugs. We demonstrate reproducible generation of stable Pickering emulsions by exposing the two-phase mixture to a probe generating Ultrasonic waves. The destabilization experiments are conducted by altering the medium pH. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to model nanoparticle–oil–water systems at the molecular scale. Through MD and coarse grain simulation we seek a mechanistic understanding of particle migration and adsorption at the oil–water interface, quantification of interfacial energy changes, and free energy barriers which need to be overcome for adsorption and desorption. In brief, this combined experimental–computational framework probes the switchable stability aspect of particle engineered emulsions. Key Words: Pickering emulsion, switchable stability
